Data Structures
Part 3: Dictionaries
Using key-value pairs instead of
indices to store grouped data.

Dictionaries and Key Value Pairs
A dictionary is a data structure
student = {
that stores information as key-
value pairs.
"name": "Alice",
Each key acts as a unique name
used to access its associated
value instead of using a "grade": 11,
numerical index.
"average": 87.5
Values can be different data
types and can be added,
removed, or changed after the
}
dictionary is created.
Dictionaries are useful when each
piece of data has a meaningful
label.

Creating a Dictionary
A dictionary is created using
student = {
curly brackets {} to surround its
contents.
"name": "Alice",
Inside the {}, each item is
written as a key-value pair, with
"grade": 11,
a colon (:) separating the key
from its value.
"average": 87.5
Multiple key-value pairs are
separated by commas (,). }
An empty dictionary can be
created using just {}.

Accessing Values with Keys
student = {
Values in a dictionary are
"name": "Alice",
accessed using their key
"grade": 11,
instead of a numerical index.
"average": 87.5
}
Place the key inside square
brackets [] after the dictionary's
print(student["name"])
variable name. print(student["grade"])
Python then returns the value
associated with that key.
OUTPUT
Alice
Each key in a dictionary must be
11
unique.

Changing Values with Keys
Dictionary values can be student = {
changed by accessing an "name": "Alice",
existing key and assigning it a "grade": 11,
new value.
"average": 87.5
}
The key is placed inside square
brackets [], followed by the student["average"] = 92.0
assignment operator = and the print(student)
new value.
This changes the value OUTPUT
{'name': 'Alice', 'grade': 11, 'average': 92.0}
associated with that key while
leaving the rest of the dictionary
unchanged.

Adding New Key-Value Pairs
student = {
A new key-value pair can be
"name": "Alice",
added to a dictionary by placing
"grade": 11
a new key inside square brackets
}
[] and assigning it a value.
student["average"] = 87.5
If the key does not already exist,
Python creates a new key-value
print(student)
pair in the dictionary.
If the key already exists, its current
value will be replaced instead. OUTPUT
{'name': 'Alice', 'grade': 11, 'average': 87.5}
This makes dictionaries easy to
expand as new information
becomes available.

pop()
Removing Items –
The pop() method removes a student = {
"name": "Alice",
key-value pair from a dictionary
"grade": 11,
using its key. "average": 87.5
}
It also returns the value that
removed = student.pop("average")
was removed, allowing it to be
stored or used elsewhere.
print(removed)
print(student)
This is useful when you know
which key you want to remove.
OUTPUT
87.5
{'name': 'Alice', 'grade': 11}

popitem()
Removing Items –
The popitem() method removes student = {
"name": "Alice",
the last key-value pair added to
"grade": 11,
a dictionary.
"average": 87.5
}
It returns the removed key and
value together as a tuple.
removed = student.popitem()
This is useful when you want to
print(removed)
remove the most recently
print(student)
added item without specifying
its key.
OUTPUT
('average', 87.5)
{'name': 'Alice', 'grade': 11}

clear()
Removing Items –
The clear() method removes student = {
"name": "Alice",
all key-value pairs from a
"grade": 11
dictionary.
}
The dictionary still exists
student.clear()
afterward, but it is empty.
This is useful when you want to print(student)
reset a dictionary and continue
using the same variable.
OUTPUT
{}

len()
Checking Length with
The len() function returns the student = {
number of key-value pairs "name": "Alice",
stored in a dictionary. "grade": 11,
"average": 87.5
Each pair counts as one item.
}
This is useful when you need to
know how many pieces of
print(len(student))
information are stored.
OUTPUT
3

get()
Dictionary Specific Methods –
The get() method retrieves the student = {
"name": "Alice",
value associated with a
"grade": 11
specified key. }
Unlike square brackets [], it print(student.get("name"))
does not cause an error if the
# Setting a default value
key does not exist.
print(student.get("average", "N/A"))
You can also provide a default
value to return when the key is
missing. OUTPUT
Alice
N/A

setdefault()
Dictionary Specific Methods –
The setdefault() method checks student = {
"name": "Alice",
whether a key already exists in a
"grade": 11
dictionary.
}
If the key exists, its current value is
returned; if it does not exist, the student.setdefault("average", 0)
key is added with a specified
default value. print(student)
This is useful when you want to
ensure that a dictionary contains
OUTPUT
a particular key without replacing
{'name': 'Alice', 'grade': 11, 'average': 0}
an existing value.

keys()
Dictionary Specific Methods –
The keys() method provides student = {
"name": "Alice",
access to all of the keys stored
"grade": 11,
in a dictionary.
"average": 87.5
It is commonly used when you }
want to traverse the labels or
for key in student.keys():
names used by the dictionary.
print(key)
The keys can be accessed with
a for loop.
OUTPUT
name
grade
average

values()
Dictionary Specific Methods –
The values() method provides student = {
"name": "Alice",
access to all of the values
"grade": 11,
stored in a dictionary.
"average": 87.5
It is useful when you only need }
the stored data and do not
for value in student.values():
need the keys.
print(value)
The values can be traversed
with a for loop.
OUTPUT
Alice
11
87.5

items()
Dictionary Specific Methods –
The items() method provides student = {
access to both the keys and "name": "Alice",
values stored in a dictionary. "grade": 11,
"average": 87.5
Each key-value pair can be
}
unpacked into two variables
while traversing the dictionary.
for key, value in student.items():
print(f"key: {key}, value: {value}")
This is useful when you need to
work with both parts of each
dictionary entry.
OUTPUT
key: name, value: Alice
key: grade, value: 11
key: average, value: 87.5

Copy vs Reference
original = {"name": "Alice", "grade": 11}
When you assign an existing dictionary
to another variable, Python does not
reference = original
create a new dictionary.
copied = original.copy()
Instead, the new variable becomes a
reference["grade"] = 12
reference to the same dictionary, copied["name"] = "Bob"
meaning both variables point to the
print(f"Original: {original}")
same data in memory and changes
print(f"Reference: {reference}")
made through either variable affect
print(f"Copy: {copied}")
both.
Using the copy() method creates a
separate dictionary that can be OUTPUT
changed without changing the original. Original: {'name': 'Alice', 'grade': 12}
Reference: {'name': 'Alice', 'grade': 12}
This is useful when you want to work
Copy: {'name': 'Bob', 'grade': 11}
with a modified version of a dictionary
while keeping the original unchanged.
